Colombo Dengue Early-Warning: ensemble learning with explainability¶

Module: Applied Machine Learning · Task: Class Activity (Lecture 7) + Final Assignment
Local problem: Will Colombo district record a high-dengue week two weeks from now?
Data: weekly notified dengue cases + climate variables, Colombo district, 2009–2014 (Epidemiology Unit, Ministry of Health, Sri Lanka; R package colmozzie, CC0).
Models: Random Forest · XGBoost · LightGBM · CatBoost · Soft Voting · Time-aware Stacking · ARIMA+RF hybrid, compared with persistence, decision tree, logistic regression and SVM baselines.
Explainability: SHAP (global + local), LIME, with a with/without-climate ablation. Deployment: pickle + Flask web app + Dockerfile.

2. Problem definition and domain context¶

Why dengue in Colombo? Dengue is a notifiable disease in Sri Lanka and the Colombo district reports one of the largest numbers of cases each year. Hospitals, the Epidemiology Unit and local councils (fogging, clean-up campaigns, bed planning) need lead time: knowing a surge is coming now is less useful than knowing about it in a couple of weeks.

Prediction task (classification). Using only information available in week t (the last four weeks of case counts, the epidemiological week, and 4-/8-week averages of rainfall, humidity, temperature, wind and visibility), predict whether the cases in week t + 2 will exceed the high-week threshold. The threshold is the 75th percentile of the training period (about 150 notified cases per week).

What the columns mean. Cases = notified dengue cases in the week; TEM/TMAX/Tm = mean/max/min temperature (°C); H = relative humidity (%); PP = precipitation (mm); SLP = sea-level pressure; VV = visibility (km); V/VM = mean / maximum sustained wind speed (km/h).

Domain knowledge used. (i) Sri Lanka has two monsoons, the south-west (about May–September) and the north-east (about December–February), and rain-filled containers and drains are Aedes breeding sites, so week-of-year is encoded cyclically; (ii) mosquito life-cycle and incubation make climate effects lagged, so we use rolling 4-/8-week climate averages rather than same-week values; (iii) notified cases are reported with a delay and are strongly autocorrelated, so recent case history is expected to dominate.

Audit findings (all would silently damage a model if ignored):

  1. SLP was read as text because one cell contains the Excel error #DIV/0!; isna() reports zero nulls, so the problem is invisible to a naive null check.
  2. Three calendar weeks are missing (2009 wk 44, 2013 wk 37–38). If left alone, shift(1) would silently turn a 2-week gap into a "1-week lag".
  3. Five weeks in 2012 report exactly 0 cases between neighbours of 38 and 64. A Colombo week with zero notified dengue cases is not credible; these are reporting gaps stored as zeros.
  4. No duplicate (Year, Week) rows.

4. Preprocessing¶

  1. Impossible zeros: 5 weeks in 2012 report 0 cases between weeks of 38 and 64 → treated as un-reported, set to missing.
  2. Type repair: SLP '#DIV/0!' → NaN (an Excel error that leaked into the CSV).
  3. Calendar repair: build a real date from ISO year-week, re-insert the missing weeks so that lags are true lags.
  4. Imputation: time-based linear interpolation (weeks are consecutive, so neighbours are informative); every imputed week is flagged.
  5. Transformations / scaling: only where they matter (see below).

# outlier screen (IQR rule) - we only *look*; extreme weather / epidemic weeks are real signal, so we keep them
num = ["Cases", "TEM", "TMAX", "Tm", "SLP", "H", "PP", "VV", "V", "VM"]
q1, q3 = weekly[num].quantile(.25), weekly[num].quantile(.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
out = ((weekly[num] < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (weekly[num] > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)).sum()
skew = weekly[num].skew()
display(pd.DataFrame({"IQR outliers": out, "skewness": skew.round(2)}).T)
print("skewness of Cases after log1p:", round(float(np.log1p(weekly['Cases']).skew()), 2),
      "| PP after log1p:", round(float(np.log1p(weekly['PP']).skew()), 2))

Decisions and why

  • Zeros → missing → time-interpolated (flagged). Treating them as real would teach the model that outbreaks randomly "switch off".
  • Cases is right-skewed (≈1.2); PP and VV are heavily skewed. Tree ensembles are invariant to monotone transforms, so no log transform is applied to their inputs. Standardisation is applied only inside the logistic-regression and SVM baselines, where scale matters.
  • Outliers are kept: heavy-rain weeks and epidemic peaks are the signal we want to predict, and trees are robust to them.
  • Cyclic encoding (sin/cos of week) so week 52 and week 1 are neighbours; cases_mean4, cases_growth, cases_trend3 capture level and momentum.

What the EDA tells us

  • Seasonality: mean cases peak in June–July (≈180–200) and again in December–January (≈140–150), with a trough in March–April (≈70). This lines up with the two monsoon periods.
  • Trend: mean weekly cases roughly doubled between 2009 and 2011–2014, so the series is non-stationary: a fixed "high week" threshold gets exceeded more often in later years, and the test period has a higher high-week rate (36%) than training (25%).
  • Memory: week-to-week autocorrelation is strong (lag-1 ≈ 0.70, lag-2 ≈ 0.63, lag-4 ≈ 0.48), so recent cases will carry most of the signal.
  • Climate: same-week correlations with cases are weak (about 0.2 or below). Lagged correlations grow to roughly 0.27 for humidity at ~7 weeks and ~0.29 for temperature at 10–12 weeks, which fits the mosquito life-cycle but is also partly confounded by seasonality and the upward trend. Because case history already integrates past weather, we expect climate to add little at a 2-week horizon; section 11 tests that expectation instead of assuming it.

6. Turning the series into a supervised problem¶

For every week t we build the 11 input fields (RAW_FIELDS, see dengue_features.py) from information available at week t only, and the label says whether cases in week t + 2 exceed the high-week threshold (75th percentile of the training period).
The last available row is held out completely for the single-sample inference demo; a chronological 75/25 split follows, with a 2-week embargo between train and test so that no label overlaps.

In [10]:
X_all, y_cases = dfx.build_supervised(weekly)               # inputs at week t, cases at t+HORIZON
X_infer, y_infer_cases = X_all.iloc[[-1]], y_cases.iloc[[-1]]  # left-out week -> single-sample inference (Step 6)
X_m, y_m_cases = X_all.iloc[:-1], y_cases.iloc[:-1]

n = len(X_m); n_train = int(n * 0.75)
X_train, X_test = X_m.iloc[:n_train], X_m.iloc[n_train + HORIZON:]          # embargo of HORIZON rows
THRESH = float(y_m_cases.iloc[:n_train].quantile(0.75))                      # defined on TRAIN only (no leakage)
y_train = (y_m_cases.iloc[:n_train] > THRESH).astype(int)
y_test = (y_m_cases.iloc[n_train + HORIZON:] > THRESH).astype(int)

7. Evaluation helpers and baselines (the "existing approaches" to beat)¶

Scaling is applied only where the algorithm needs it (logistic regression, SVM). Tree ensembles are scale-invariant, so they get raw features.

In [12]:
def make_pipe(model, scale=False):
    steps = [("features", FunctionTransformer(add_derived))]
    if scale: steps.append(("scaler", StandardScaler()))
    return Pipeline(steps + [("model", model)])

def block_bootstrap_auc(y, p, block=4, B=2000, seed=SEED):
    """95% CI for AUC with a moving-block bootstrap (weeks are autocorrelated, so plain resampling is too optimistic)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); y, p = np.asarray(y), np.asarray(p); n = len(y); aucs = []
    for _ in range(B):
        idx = np.concatenate([np.arange(s, s + block) % n for s in rng.integers(0, n, int(np.ceil(n / block)))])[:n]
        if 0 < y[idx].sum() < n: aucs.append(roc_auc_score(y[idx], p[idx]))
    return np.percentile(aucs, [2.5, 97.5])

results, test_scores, cv_scores = {}, {}, {}
def evaluate(name, score, y, pred=None, thr=0.5):
    pred = (np.asarray(score) >= thr).astype(int) if pred is None else pred
    lo, hi = block_bootstrap_auc(y, score)
    test_scores[name] = np.asarray(score)
    results[name] = dict(test_auc=roc_auc_score(y, score), auc_lo=lo, auc_hi=hi, test_pr_auc=average_precision_score(y, score),
                         recall=recall_score(y, pred), precision=precision_score(y, pred, zero_division=0),
                         f1=f1_score(y, pred), accuracy=accuracy_score(y, pred))
    return results[name]

def cv_auc(pipe):
    s = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=tscv, scoring="roc_auc"); return s.mean(), s.std()
In [13]:
models = {}   # fitted pipelines (train only)

# --- 7a. Persistence rule: "if this week is already high, 2 weeks from now will be high" ---
folds = [roc_auc_score(y_train.iloc[v], X_train["cases_t"].iloc[v]) for _, v in tscv.split(X_train)]
cv_scores["Persistence rule"] = (np.mean(folds), np.std(folds))
evaluate("Persistence rule", X_test["cases_t"].values, y_test, pred=(X_test["cases_t"] > THRESH).astype(int).values)

# --- 7b. Classical models (tuned with the same time-aware CV, so the comparison is fair) ---
baselines = {
    "Decision Tree": (DecisionTreeClassifier(class_weight="balanced", random_state=SEED), False,
                      {"model__max_depth": [2, 3, 4, 5], "model__min_samples_leaf": [5, 10, 20]}),
    "Logistic Regression": (LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=2000), True,
                            {"model__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}),
    "SVM (RBF)": (SVC(probability=True, class_weight="balanced", random_state=SEED), True,
                  {"model__C": [0.1, 1, 10], "model__gamma": ["scale", 0.01, 0.1]}),
}
for name, (est, scale, grid) in baselines.items():
    gs = GridSearchCV(make_pipe(est, scale), grid, cv=tscv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_train, y_train)
    models[name] = gs.best_estimator_
    cv_scores[name] = (gs.best_score_, gs.cv_results_["std_test_score"][gs.best_index_])
    evaluate(name, gs.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1], y_test)
    print(f"{name:20s} CV AUC {gs.best_score_:.3f}  best: {gs.best_params_}")

8. Parameter engineering (no default values)¶

The data is small (204 training weeks, ~50 high weeks) and autocorrelated, so the main risk is over-fitting. Every search space below is built around that:

Model Hyper-parameter Range tried Reasoning
Random Forest max_depth 3–8 shallow trees; deep trees memorise 200 rows
min_samples_leaf 3–12 forces each leaf to cover several weeks → smoother probabilities
max_features sqrt / 0.4 / 0.6 decorrelates trees; several features are near-duplicates (lags, rolling means)
max_samples 0.6 / 0.8 / all stronger bagging → lower variance
class_weight balanced(+subsample) high weeks are only 25% of the data
n_estimators 200–800 more trees never hurt a forest, they only cost time
XGBoost learning_rate × n_estimators 0.01–0.1 × 150–600 small steps with early-stopped depth; the two are traded off
max_depth 2–4 weak learners; interactions of 2–3 features are enough
min_child_weight, gamma 1–8, 0–3 refuse splits supported by too few weeks
subsample, colsample_bytree 0.6–1, 0.5–0.9 stochastic boosting as regularisation
reg_lambda 1–20 L2 shrinkage of leaf weights
scale_pos_weight 1–3 imbalance (≈3 negatives per positive)
LightGBM num_leaves, max_depth, min_child_samples 4–12, 3–4, 5–25 leaf-wise growth overfits quickly on tiny data, so cap it
CatBoost depth, l2_leaf_reg, auto_class_weights 3–5, 3–10, Balanced symmetric trees are already regularised; keep them shallow

Search method: randomised search (30–40 draws; 12 for CatBoost) scored by ROC-AUC with an expanding-window TimeSeriesSplit (5 folds, gap = 2 weeks). A shuffled K-fold would let the model train on weeks after the ones it is validated on, which flatters the score.

In [14]:
def tune(name, est, space, n_iter):
    t0 = time.time()
    rs = RandomizedSearchCV(make_pipe(est), {f"model__{k}": v for k, v in space.items()}, n_iter=n_iter, cv=tscv,
                            scoring="roc_auc", random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_train, y_train)
    models[name] = rs.best_estimator_
    cv_scores[name] = (rs.best_score_, rs.cv_results_["std_test_score"][rs.best_index_])
    evaluate(name, rs.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1], y_test)
    print(f"{name:14s} CV AUC {rs.best_score_:.3f} +/- {cv_scores[name][1]:.3f}   ({time.time()-t0:.0f}s)")
    print("   ", {k.replace('model__', ''): v for k, v in rs.best_params_.items()}); return rs

rf_space = dict(n_estimators=[200, 400, 600, 800], max_depth=[3, 4, 5, 6, 8], min_samples_leaf=[3, 5, 8, 12],
                max_features=["sqrt", 0.4, 0.6], max_samples=[0.6, 0.8, None], class_weight=["balanced", "balanced_subsample"])
xgb_space = dict(n_estimators=[150, 250, 400, 600], learning_rate=[0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1], max_depth=[2, 3, 4],
                 min_child_weight=[1, 3, 5, 8], subsample=[0.6, 0.8, 1.0], colsample_bytree=[0.5, 0.7, 0.9],
                 reg_lambda=[1, 5, 10, 20], gamma=[0, 0.5, 1, 3], scale_pos_weight=[1, 2, 3])
lgbm_space = dict(n_estimators=[150, 300, 500], learning_rate=[0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1], num_leaves=[4, 6, 8, 12], max_depth=[3, 4],
                  min_child_samples=[5, 10, 15, 25], subsample=[0.6, 0.8, 1.0], colsample_bytree=[0.5, 0.7, 0.9],
                  reg_lambda=[0, 5, 10], class_weight=["balanced", None])

                 auto_class_weights=["Balanced", None])

rs_rf = tune("Random Forest", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1), rf_space, 30)
rs_xgb = tune("XGBoost", XGBClassifier(eval_metric="logloss", tree_method="hist", random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1), xgb_space, 40)
rs_lgbm = tune("LightGBM", LGBMClassifier(subsample_freq=1, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1, verbose=-1), lgbm_space, 30)
rs_cat = tune("CatBoost", CatBoostClassifier(random_seed=SEED, verbose=0, thread_count=1, allow_writing_files=False), cat_space, 12)

9. Ensembling: soft voting and time-aware stacking¶

  • Soft voting (the shared-notebook pipeline from the activity guideline): average the predicted probabilities of the tuned Random Forest and XGBoost.
  • Stacking: the four tuned tree ensembles are base learners; a logistic-regression meta-learner is trained on their out-of-fold probabilities. Folds are expanding-window (see TimeAwareStacking), because ordinary K-fold would let the meta-learner see the future.
In [15]:
rf_best = clone(models["Random Forest"].named_steps["model"]); xgb_best = clone(models["XGBoost"].named_steps["model"])
lgbm_best = clone(models["LightGBM"].named_steps["model"]); cat_best = clone(models["CatBoost"].named_steps["model"])

voting = make_pipe(VotingClassifier([("rf", rf_best), ("xgb", xgb_best)], voting="soft"))
stack = make_pipe(TimeAwareStacking([("rf", rf_best), ("xgb", xgb_best), ("lgbm", lgbm_best), ("cat", cat_best)], gap=HORIZON))
for name, p in {"Soft Voting (RF+XGB)": voting, "Stacking (4 models)": stack}.items():
    cv_scores[name] = cv_auc(p)
    models[name] = p.fit(X_train, y_train)
    evaluate(name, p.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1], y_test)
    print(f"{name:22s} CV AUC {cv_scores[name][0]:.3f} +/- {cv_scores[name][1]:.3f}")
print("meta-learner weights on [RF, XGB, LGBM, Cat] probabilities:", models["Stacking (4 models)"].named_steps["model"].meta_.coef_.round(2))

10. Extension: ARIMA + Random Forest hybrid (time-series stacking idea from the lecture)¶

ARIMA captures the autoregressive structure of the case series; its 2-week forecast becomes an extra feature for the Random Forest. For the row at week t ARIMA is fitted only on data up to week t, so there is no leakage. This variant needs the full case history, so it is evaluated here but not deployed in the 11-field web form.

In [16]:
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
log_c = np.log1p(weekly["Cases"])
train_end = weekly.index.get_loc(X_train.index[-1]) + 1
import warnings as _w
aic = {}
with _w.catch_warnings():
    _w.simplefilter("ignore")
    for p in range(3):
        for q in range(3):
            try: aic[(p, 1, q)] = ARIMA(log_c.iloc[:train_end].values, order=(p, 1, q)).fit().aic
            except Exception: pass
order = min(aic, key=aic.get); print("ARIMA order chosen by AIC on the training period:", order)

def arima_fc(pos, h=HORIZON):
    with _w.catch_warnings():
        _w.simplefilter("ignore")
        try: return float(np.expm1(ARIMA(log_c.iloc[:pos + 1].values, order=order).fit().forecast(h)[-1]))
        except Exception: return float(weekly["Cases"].iloc[pos])
t0 = time.time()
arima_feat = pd.Series([arima_fc(weekly.index.get_loc(d)) for d in X_all.index], index=X_all.index, name="arima_fc")
print(f"{len(arima_feat)} rolling ARIMA fits in {time.time()-t0:.0f}s")

X_hyb = X_all.assign(arima_fc=arima_feat)
hyb = make_pipe(clone(rf_best))
s = cross_val_score(hyb, X_hyb.loc[X_train.index], y_train, cv=tscv, scoring="roc_auc"); cv_scores["ARIMA + RF hybrid"] = (s.mean(), s.std())
hyb.fit(X_hyb.loc[X_train.index], y_train); models["ARIMA + RF hybrid"] = hyb
evaluate("ARIMA + RF hybrid", hyb.predict_proba(X_hyb.loc[X_test.index])[:, 1], y_test)
print("ARIMA forecast alone as a score -> test AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, X_hyb.loc[X_test.index, "arima_fc"]), 3))

11. Performance comparison¶

CV AUC = mean ± std over 5 expanding-window folds on the training period (this is what model selection uses). Test metrics come from the untouched final 66 weeks; the AUC interval is a block-bootstrap 95% CI. Precision/recall/F1 use the default 0.5 cut-off.

Does climate help? (ablation)¶

Domain knowledge says climate matters; the EDA suggests case history dominates. We re-train the same tuned RF and XGBoost with the six climate fields removed.

In [19]:
def no_climate(X): return add_derived(X).drop(columns=CLIMATE_FIELDS)

for name in ["Random Forest", "XGBoost"]:
    p = Pipeline([("features", FunctionTransformer(no_climate)), ("model", clone(models[name].named_steps["model"]))])
    s = cross_val_score(p, X_train, y_train, cv=tscv, scoring="roc_auc"); p.fit(X_train, y_train)
    pr = p.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    abl[name] = dict(cv_with_climate=cv_scores[name][0], cv_without=s.mean(), test_with_climate=results[name]["test_auc"], test_without=roc_auc_score(y_test, pr))

Interpretation of the comparison¶

Headline numbers (final run). Cross-validated AUC: XGBoost 0.832, logistic regression 0.822, SVM 0.820, soft voting 0.815, Random Forest 0.809, LightGBM 0.806, ARIMA+RF 0.802, stacking 0.797, CatBoost 0.782, persistence rule 0.758, decision tree 0.707. On the untouched test weeks the tuned ensembles reach AUC ≈ 0.77–0.81 versus 0.72 for persistence and 0.70 for the single tree.

What we can and cannot conclude

  • The ensembles clearly beat the simplest approaches (single decision tree, persistence rule) on both CV and test.
  • They do not clearly beat a well-regularised logistic regression or SVM in CV (0.82 vs 0.83), and the test AUC confidence intervals (roughly 0.65–0.92, width ≈ 0.25) overlap for almost every model. With ~66 test weeks and a fold-to-fold CV spread of about 0.1, the ranking among the ensembles is not statistically meaningful. The honest statement is: "tree ensembles are at least as good as, and on the test weeks somewhat better than, linear baselines, and far better than naive rules".
  • Stacking and the ARIMA hybrid did not help. With ~200 rows the meta-learner has little to learn from, and extra complexity buys variance, not bias reduction. ARIMA alone is a weak predictor of a threshold event (test AUC 0.71).
  • Climate adds no reliable value: CV AUC is 0.809 vs 0.808 (RF) and 0.832 vs 0.813 (XGB) with vs without climate, while the test AUC is slightly higher without climate for both. Mixed evidence in both directions = no demonstrable benefit at a 2-week horizon with this much data.
  • Model selection rule: XGBoost has the best CV AUC among the ensembles (and overall), so it is deployed. Logistic regression is the main rival; it is reported in full, and it is not the deployment choice only because the brief asks for an ensemble solution and its test AUC (0.75) is lower.

Strengths and limitations of each model (in this problem)

Model Strengths seen here Limitations seen here
Random Forest stable, hardly sensitive to hyper-parameters; best test PR-AUC (0.75); bagging copes with noisy climate columns probabilities are compressed toward the middle; ignores ordering of time; large files if many trees
XGBoost best CV AUC; native class weighting; strong regularisation controls most hyper-parameters to tune; easy to over-fit 200 rows; lower test AUC than RF (0.79 vs 0.81), within noise
LightGBM / CatBoost fast; CatBoost's symmetric trees are a good small-data prior LightGBM leaf-wise growth is fragile at this size; CatBoost's categorical strengths are unused (no categorical fields)
Soft voting simple, averages out RF/XGB errors, test AUC 0.80 not better than its best member in CV
Time-aware stacking principled (no future leakage), highest recall (0.79) lowest precision, meta-learner has too little data; CV 0.80
ARIMA + RF captures autoregressive structure explicitly needs the whole case history, so it cannot be served through a 11-field form
Logistic regression / SVM strong baselines, very cheap, hard to over-fit cannot model the monsoon seasonality and non-linear threshold effects; lower precision/recall balance on test
Decision tree / persistence transparent clearly the weakest

Operating point. Alerts are a trade-off: with the deployed model on the test weeks a cut-off of 0.3 catches 83% of high weeks (precision 0.54), while 0.5 catches 62% at precision 0.68. For public health, missing a surge is costlier than a false alarm, so the web app uses three bands (LOW < 25%, ELEVATED 25–50%, HIGH ≥ 50%) instead of a single yes/no.

Choosing the final model and looking at errors¶

Selection rule (uses cross-validation on the training period only, never the test set): the ensemble model with the highest cross-validated AUC, because the brief asks for an ensemble deliverable and treats logistic regression / SVM / single trees as the comparison baselines. The ARIMA hybrid is excluded because it needs the full case history.

12. Explainability (SHAP and LIME)¶

A bare probability is not enough for a public-health officer, so we open the black box. SHAP gives global importance (which fields drive the model overall) and local attributions (why this particular week was flagged). LIME is a second, independent local explanation used as a cross-check. SHAP is computed for the tuned Random Forest and XGBoost on the test weeks (RF values are in probability units, XGBoost in log-odds).

In [21]:
def tree_shap(pipe, X):
    Xf = pipe.named_steps["features"].transform(X)
    sv = shap.TreeExplainer(pipe.named_steps["model"])(Xf)
    return Xf, (sv[:, :, 1] if sv.values.ndim == 3 else sv)

Xf_test, sv_rf = tree_shap(models["Random Forest"], X_test)
_, sv_xgb = tree_shap(models["XGBoost"], X_test)

plt.figure(); shap.plots.beeswarm(sv_rf, max_display=12, show=False); plt.title("SHAP summary - Random Forest (test weeks)")
plt.savefig(FIG / "09_shap_beeswarm_rf.png", bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
plt.figure(); shap.plots.beeswarm(sv_xgb, max_display=12, show=False); plt.title("SHAP summary - XGBoost (test weeks)")
plt.savefig(FIG / "10_shap_beeswarm_xgb.png", bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

What SHAP shows¶

  • Case history and seasonality drive the model. The largest attributions belong to the recent case counts (cases_t1 is the top driver, then cases_t, cases_t3) and the monsoon-season encoding (week_cos, week_sin). Higher recent counts push the risk up, which is the epidemiologically sensible direction.
  • The two models agree on the ranking (Spearman ρ = 0.91 between RF and XGBoost importances), which makes the explanation more trustworthy than either alone.
  • Climate gets non-zero attribution (≈21% of the total for RF, ≈35% for XGBoost), mostly humidity and rainfall averages. This does not contradict the ablation. SHAP explains what the model uses, not whether using it helps out of sample; removing climate did not reduce test performance, so these contributions are mostly harmless noise-fitting or proxies for season. This is a good example of why importance plots must be paired with an ablation.
  • The dependence plot for the top driver (cases_t1) shows a step-like jump at about 150 cases, i.e. exactly the high-week threshold, then a plateau: the model has essentially learned "was last week already a high week?", refined by season.

13. Final model, single-sample inference (the left-out week) and local explanations¶

The chosen pipeline is refit on all modelling weeks (train + test, same hyper-parameters) for deployment. The left-out week was never used anywhere.

    plt.figure(); shap.plots.waterfall(sv_i[0], max_display=10, show=False); plt.title(f"Local SHAP - {k} - week of {X_infer.index[0].date()}")
    plt.savefig(FIG / f"13_shap_waterfall_{k.split()[0].lower()}.png", bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

Reading the single-sample inference¶

The left-out week (starting 5 May 2014) had 146 cases that week, 115, 159 and 42 in the three weeks before, so recent counts were around the 150 threshold but the 4-week average was modest. Two weeks later there were 329 cases, the start of the largest surge in the data. The deployed model gave a probability of only ~11%, so it missed this surge (a false negative).

Why (XGBoost SHAP waterfall): the calendar position (week_sin, week_cos: early May is before the usual June–July peak) and last week's count of 115, below the threshold, pulled the score down the most, followed by the modest growth ratio and the low count three weeks earlier; only the 8-week rainfall nudged it up. LIME agrees in direction (low cases_t3 and the mid-range case counts lower the risk). A jump from ~150 to ~330 in two weeks is an explosive outbreak that no 4-week summary of the previous weeks can foresee. This is a real limitation to report: the model anticipates sustained high periods much better than sudden explosive surges. The web app therefore includes this week as a "hard case" button next to a correctly flagged rising week (p ≈ 0.96) and a correctly cleared quiet week (p ≈ 0.04).

LIME's local linear fit has a low R² (≈0.08), so its weights are only a rough second opinion; SHAP (exact for tree models) is the primary explanation.

15. Front end (GenAI-generated) and deployment¶

The prompt used to generate the interface is in prompts/frontend_prompt.md. It follows the lecturer's recipe: describe the pickled model, list the exact input fields, ask for a pickle loader and a small UI with text boxes.

pip install -r requirements.txt
python app/app.py              # http://localhost:5000  (form, JSON API at POST /predict)
# production / bonus marks: Docker image runs gunicorn on $PORT
docker build -t dengue-ew . && docker run -p 8080:8080 dengue-ew

The same container deploys unchanged to Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, Render or AWS App Runner (see README).

16. Conclusions, limitations and next steps¶

Conclusions

  1. Tuned tree ensembles predict a high-dengue week two weeks ahead with AUC ≈ 0.8 (95% CI roughly 0.65–0.9) and clearly outperform naive rules and a single tree; their advantage over regularised linear models is small and not statistically established on this dataset.
  2. Case history and monsoon seasonality carry nearly all the predictive value; climate adds none that we could demonstrate.
  3. SHAP gives a consistent, epidemiologically plausible explanation across two different models; LIME is a weak secondary check.
  4. The model cannot anticipate sudden explosive surges (left-out week), so it is a decision-support signal, not an autonomous alarm.

Limitations. Only ~270 weekly rows from one district and 5 years; one train/test split; threshold and seasonality assumptions drift over time (non-stationary trend); notified cases ≠ true incidence; 5 zero weeks were assumed to be reporting gaps; no confirmation from the Epidemiology Unit.

Next steps. Add more districts and years (the denguedatahub package covers more Sri Lankan weeks), add lagged local weather from the Department of Meteorology, try counterfactual explanations (DiCE) and a regression target (expected cases) with quantile loss, and monitor drift with the MLOps pipeline from the previous lectures.

Reproducibility: seeds are fixed (42); executed with the library versions listed in requirements.txt.
